name: Berdazimer gel

lead: Berdazimer gel (Zelsuvmi) is a prescription gel for molluscum contagiosum, the small raised bumps caused by a virus. Applied once daily to the lesions for up to 12 weeks, it releases nitric oxide.
People use it to clear the bumps and return the skin to a smooth, even look. It was FDA authorized in January 2024 for ages one and up.

paras: The gel releases nitric oxide on the skin, which has antiviral properties. The exact way it clears molluscum is described as not fully understood.
The most common effects are burning, itching, redness and irritation where it is applied. It is available by prescription in the US.

angle.text: Berdazimer gel is applied daily to molluscum bumps, and in trials a larger share of treated participants reached complete clearance than with vehicle gel. Clearing the bumps removes a visible skin-texture concern, and the trials also tracked scarring.

lead: Berdazimer gel, sold as Zelsuvmi, is a prescription topical medicine that releases nitric oxide onto the skin to clear molluscum contagiosum, the small, dome-shaped bumps caused by a poxvirus. By clearing these visible lesions, it helps restore smooth, even-looking skin, particularly for children and for adults whose bumps are conspicuous.[1][2]

The FDA authorized Zelsuvmi on January 5, 2024 for people aged one year and older; it is described as the first licensed prescription medication for molluscum that is applied at home.[2] It is applied once daily to lesions for up to 12 weeks and is supplied as two components, a berdazimer gel and a hydrogel, that are combined for use.[2]

Efficacy was examined in vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials, including the 891-participant B-SIMPLE4 study, and in a meta-analysis of four randomized trials with 1,854 patients.[3][1] The most common side effects are local: burning, itching, redness and irritation at the application site.[2]

paras: Berdazimer gel is indicated for molluscum contagiosum in patients aged one year and older.[2] The condition is a common viral skin infection, mostly in children, with lesions that can last months to years and may cause itching, self-consciousness and household spread.[4][5]

In the phase 3 B-SIMPLE4 trial, 891 participants aged six months and older with 3 to 70 lesions applied berdazimer 10.3% gel or vehicle gel once daily for 12 weeks; the primary endpoint was complete clearance at week 12.[3][6] A meta-analysis of randomized trials found berdazimer effective for lesion clearance and reported reduced scarring, while noting a higher rate of topical adverse effects that matters particularly for children.[1]

An integrated analysis of three randomized trials, a trial in people with atopic dermatitis, a pharmacokinetic study and a Japanese open-label study have also been published.[7][8][9][10] A systematic review of molluscum treatments describes berdazimer's safety profile as favorable for pediatric patients, and a review on adherence notes that daily topical treatments face adherence challenges.[11][12]

The gel generates nitric oxide, which has antiviral properties; the exact mechanism in molluscum is described as unclear but thought to involve inflammation, immune regulation and viral replication.[2] Laboratory work has examined its effect on the molluscum virus in vitro.[13]
Reported effects are mostly at the application site, including burning, itching, redness and irritation.[2]

timeline.event: Phase 3 B-SIMPLE1 and B-SIMPLE2 trials begin.[14][15]
FDA authorizes Zelsuvmi for molluscum in people aged one year and older.[2]
